item.title: 7. Testing With Local Database
item.description:
Local Database lets you try your project on a Postgres database on your own computer before you ship it. You can build the tables, fill them with sample rows, run queries, and start the exported API, all from one window.You'll need: PostgreSQL running on your computer the .NET SDK (8 or newer) for Start API and NodeWalker's Run button Installing Postgres and the .NET SDK will get its own tutorial. Until then, the official installers from postgresql.org and dot.net work fine with the default settings. Open Local Database from the desktop while a project is open. The window works top to bottom.The box starts with:Host=localhost;Port=5432;Username=postgres;Password=;Database=dd_dev Put in your own password (and change the database name if you like), then press Test & save. The connection is saved inside the project, encrypted like the rest of it, and the database is created if it doesn't exist yet.The connection is never included when you export or share the project.Both buttons use your latest Build Project export, so build first. Create from scratch drops this project's schemas and runs SQL.sql and then RLS.sql. Use it the first time, or whenever you want a clean start.
Apply Migration.sql upgrades a database built from the previous export and keeps its data. See 8. Migrations. Pick how many rows per table you want and press Add sample data. The rows look like real data (names, emails, prices, dates) and follow your rules: Parent tables are filled first, so foreign keys always point at real rows. Unique columns stay unique. Lengths, Not Null and CHECK (column IN (...)) lists are respected. The rows are also saved as SampleData.sql in the export folder.Type SQL in the query box and press Run (Ctrl+Enter). Results show in a grid (the first 200 rows).INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are rolled back afterwards, so you can experiment freely. Tick Keep changes if you want them to stay.Start API runs the exported API with dotnet run against this database at http://localhost:5180 and opens Swagger, where you can call every route from the browser. Open Swagger opens it again, and Stop shuts the API down.The first start takes a little while because .NET has to download packages and compile.
You don't have to start the whole API to test one function. In NodeWalker, ▶ Run runs just the graph you're editing against this database. See 2. NODEWLKR.
💜 Break it on purpose! This database is yours to wreck, so go try the weird stuff. Order 0 items. Order more than there is in stock. Delete a user who has orders. If something goes through that shouldn't, it's way better to find out here than after you ship it, dummy.
item.guid: Tutorials For Building/7. Testing With Local Database.md

item.title: 13. Notes, ER Diagram And Import SQL
item.description:
Three desktop apps that help while you design: Notes for keeping track of things, ER Diagram for seeing the whole database at once, and Import SQL for bringing in a database you already have.All three need a project to be open.Notes keeps notes inside your project, so your to-do list and design ideas stay with the tables they're about. + New makes a note. Type its title in the box at the top and the note itself underneath. Notes save by themselves as you type. Pin keeps a note at the top of the list. Type in Search notes... to find a note by its title or text. Pick a table in the Table box to link the note to that table. Lines that start with [ ] or [x] become checklist items. [x] Add products table [ ] Add RLS for orders [ ] Try checkout on Local Database Notes are encrypted with the rest of the project, and they're included when you export it. The text box fills the window and scrolls, so long notes are fine.
ER Diagram draws every table as a card with its columns, and an arrow for every reference. Columns are marked PK (primary key), FK (foreign key) and UQ (unique). Drag a card by its title to move it. Your layout is saved with the project. Auto layout puts everything back in neat rows. The - and + buttons zoom out and in, and 100% resets the zoom. Click a card's title to open that table. Export SVG and Export PNG save a picture of the diagram to Exports\ER Diagrams and open the folder. SVG stays sharp at any size; PNG is easier to paste into chats and documents. It's the quickest way to spot a reference pointing at the wrong table, or a table that isn't connected to anything.
Already have a Postgres database? Import SQL turns its schema into tables in your project. Paste the SQL into the box on the left, or press Load .sql file.... A pg_dump --schema-only file works. Check the preview on the right. It lists every table it found, and anything it skipped. Set the Default schema for tables that don't name one (usually public). Tick Replace tables that already exist if you want imported tables to overwrite ones with the same name. Otherwise they're skipped. Press Add to project. It reads tables, columns, defaults, primary keys, foreign keys, unique and check constraints, indexes and comments. Functions, triggers, grants and data are skipped and listed, so you can see what was left out.Afterwards, run Build Project > Build Check to see if anything needs fixing, like reserved words or column names with capital letters.
💜 Moving in? Bring your stuff! Got a database from some other project? Don't you dare rebuild it table by table. Dump the schema, import it, and you're done in a minute. Then go fix whatever Build Check yells at you about.
item.guid: Tutorials For Users/13. Notes, ER Diagram And Import SQL.md

item.title: 12. Designing Your API With The API Editor
item.description:
Your database holds the data, and your API is how apps and websites talk to it. The API Editor lets you plan that API: group related routes into modules, give each module its endpoints, and give each endpoint the functions (the actual GET, POST and so on) that do the work. When you build your project, this becomes a real ASP.NET Core API with Swagger.From the main desktop, open the API Editor app. Like the RLS Editor, it works in three steps: Modules, then Endpoints, then Functions.
💜 Modules are just folders for your routes. A module is nothing scary. It's a bucket of related endpoints. Everything about signing in goes in Auth, everything about accounts goes in Users, and so on. Organize now, thank yourself later. The editor starts with four modules: Auth Users Data Admin You can rename them, give them a description and an icon, and add or remove modules as you need. Pick a module and move on to its Endpoints.
An endpoint is one area inside the module, like Login, Profile or Orders. Give each one a description, then move on to its Functions.
A function is one thing the endpoint can do. Each function has:

💜 Pick the right verb. Quick rule of thumb: GET reads, POST creates, PUT/PATCH updates, DELETE removes. Get these right and your API is easy to guess. The colors in the editor make a wrong verb jump right out.

Each function's logic is built in NodeWalker. Press Open in NodeWalker on a function, and wire up what it does: read from a table, check the input, save something, return a result. See 2. NODEWLKR for how.
You can test a function straight away with ▶ Run in NodeWalker, once you've set up 7. Testing With Local Database.When you build the project, each function becomes a route:POST api/<module>/<endpoint>/<function> Names are lower-cased and spaces become dashes, so the Cancel function under Orders in the Store module is POST api/store/orders/cancel. The inputs of its NodeWalker graph become the route's parameters.Functions without a graph still get a route. It answers "Not implemented yet" until you build the logic.
To run the API, press Start API in Local Database, or see 3. No Code API for running it yourself.Press Save to store your API design. It's kept with your project, so it's included when you export or make a template (together with the NodeWalker graphs), and it loads again the next time you open the API Editor. Group by feature, not by table. An Auth module can touch several tables, and that's fine. One function, one job. Small functions are easier to build and to test. Match verbs to what the function does, so the API and Swagger stay predictable. Keep names short and clear. They become your route names.
item.guid: Tutorials For Users/12. Designing Your API With The API Editor.md

item.title: 11. Securing Your Data With The RLS Editor
item.description:
Row Level Security (RLS) decides who can see or change which rows in your tables. Instead of every user being able to read everything, you set rules like "a user can only read their own profile" or "only admins can delete posts". The RLS Editor lets you lay that out per role and per table, and the build turns it into real Postgres policies.From the main desktop, open the RLS Editor app.
It works in three steps: Roles, then Tables, then Policies. Use the Next and Back buttons at the bottom to move between them.
💜 Think in roles first! RLS is easiest when you start from who's asking. A "Standard User" and an "Admin" should almost never have the same permissions. Get your roles right and the policies mostly write themselves. The editor starts with four common roles: Standard Users Admin Users Moderator Users Bot Users You can rename them, give them a description and an icon, and add or remove roles to match your app. Pick a role, then press Next: Tables.Admins and moderators are special: admins can read and write every row, and moderators can read every row. You don't need to write policies for that.Choose which tables this role has policies on, and give each one a description so you remember what it's protecting. Pick a table and press Next: Policies.A policy is one rule for this role on this table. Type a name and press Add Policy, then set:The Access options:Under each policy is a line that says in plain words what it allows, for example "standard_users may SELECT only rows where user_id = the current user". If it warns that there's no owner column, set one, or only admins will see those rows.
💜 One policy, one idea. Keep each policy focused. "Read own orders" and "Everyone can read products" are two policies, not one giant tangled one. Small rules are easier to read, test and fix later. Press Save to store your RLS design. It's kept with your project, so it's included when you export or make a template, and it loads again the next time you open the RLS Editor.
When you build the project, everything here becomes RLS.sql. How that file works, and how your API tells the database who's asking, is in 4. No Code RLS. Deny by default. Only add policies for what a role should be able to do; anything you don't allow stays locked. Name policies for what they allow. "Edit own comments" beats "policy_3". Use the same categories across tables so big projects stay easy to scan. Check again after adding tables. A new table with no policies for a role means that role gets nothing from it. Run Build Check. It warns about policies for tables that don't exist and tables with no owner column.
item.guid: Tutorials For Users/11. Securing Your Data With The RLS Editor.md

item.title: 8. Best Practices
item.description:
Databases are like towers; follow these tips to ensure you have a good foundation and don't end up needing to remake everything. Aim for at least 3NF (Third Normal Form) unless you have a specific reason to denormalize (e.g., read performance in reporting). PLEASE READ 9. Understanding 3NF Eliminate redundant data by splitting related information into separate tables. Use reference columns (foreign keys) instead of duplicating values. Tip: The designer’s reference validation on build will catch broken or dangling references early. Use lower-case snake_case for tables and columns (e.g., user_profile, email_address). Postgres lower-cases any name you don't quote, so UserProfile quietly becomes userprofile, and Build Check warns about capital letters for that reason. The exported C# still uses PascalCase (UserProfile, EmailAddress) for you. Column names should be clear and descriptive (e.g., email_address instead of str). Group related tables with a common schema (e.g., auth.users, auth.roles, auth.permissions). Avoid reserved words like order, user and group. Build Check flags them; use order_id or user_name instead. Every table should have a single, stable primary key. Prefer surrogate keys (e.g., an id column of type BigSerial) over natural keys for simplicity and performance. Mark the primary key column with Is Primary checked. Use Is Unique + Is Not Null for natural keys when needed. Enforce data integrity at the database level: NOT NULL for required fields UNIQUE for alternate keys (e.g., username, email) CHECK constraints for simple domain rules (e.g., age >= 0 AND age <= 150) Default values for common fallbacks (e.g., created_at DEFAULT now()) The designer supports all of these directly in the row editor. Add indexes on: Foreign key columns (improves joins) Columns used in WHERE, ORDER BY, or GROUP BY clauses Frequently searched text fields (consider GIN for JSONB or full-text) Avoid over-indexing. Each index slows down writes a little. Use the Add Index option to create composite or partial indexes when needed. Design one-to-many, many-to-many, and one-to-one relationships using reference columns. Set appropriate On Delete / On Update actions (e.g., CASCADE, RESTRICT, SET NULL). Check your relationships in the ER Diagram before building. Broken references will block export. Fill in Table Description and Column Description fields. Exported Markdown documentation pulls directly from these, so good habits here save time later. When creating templates, add rich overviews and per-table descriptions for future users. For file uploads or sensitive binary data: Use the built-in SecureMedia and SecureMediaSession types. Mark columns as Media or Encrypted (Non-Media) as appropriate. This ensures encryption at rest and controlled access patterns. It is however a custom type, so if you know what you're doing you can select something like bytes and set it to an array. Run Build Check frequently during design. Fix all validation errors before exporting. This prevents runtime surprises.
Test your build with Local Database before you ship: build the tables, add sample data and try your API (see 7. Testing With Local Database).
After the first release, upgrade with Migration.sql instead of rebuilding the database (see 8. Migrations). Create Row Templates for common patterns (e.g., Audit fields, Soft-delete, Multilingual). Create Project Templates for full application blueprints (e.g., Blog CMS, E-commerce core). Version your templates. The tool counts up v1, v2 and so on for you. Use appropriate data types (e.g., INTEGER instead of BIGINT unless needed). Prefer fixed-length types when possible (e.g., CHAR(2) for country codes). For large text, consider TEXT over VARCHAR without limit. Enable array types only when truly needed, since they can complicate queries. Design with future changes in mind: Add new columns as nullable first Use soft-delete (is_deleted BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE) instead of hard deletes Version configuration tables rather than altering core schema Use a paper and pencil to draft what you want to do before you do it. Using PsuedoCode to draft out a template of what you want to have working and figuring out the limitations + things to set for future updates (Even if you don't actively use them yet) is always a SSS+ By following these practices, your databases will be cleaner, safer, faster, and much easier to maintain as your application grows.

item.title: 6. Troubleshooting
item.description: Your firewall is probably blocking the background security service. Allow Database Designer.exe and Assets/Pariah API/Pariah API.exe through it.Usually a wrong password. It can also mean Database Designer can't write to the folder it's installed in, or the background service didn't start. Restart the app and try again. If you've forgotten your password, use Forgot Password? / Change Password on the login screen with your recovery code.Click an error to open the table it's about. The most common ones: No primary key: tick Is Primary on one column (usually id). Foreign key type mismatch: the column and the column it points at must have the same type, for example both bigint. Foreign key target isn't unique: a reference has to point at a primary key or a column marked Unique. Reserved word: rename columns like order or user to order_id or user_name. Check that Postgres is running. Check the host, port, username and password. The user needs permission to create databases the first time, because Test & save creates the database if it doesn't exist. Both need the .NET SDK. Open a terminal and run dotnet --version. If that fails, install the SDK (8 or newer) and restart Database Designer. Superusers (like postgres) and roles with BYPASSRLS skip every policy. Connect your API with a normal role that is a member of the generated roles. Check that RLS is on: SELECT relrowsecurity FROM pg_class WHERE relname = 'tablename'; Make sure your graphs use DB: RLS Set User and DB: RLS Set Role before reading or writing. Check the line under each policy in the RLS Editor. If it warns about a missing owner column, only admins can see those rows. Routes are built from the module, endpoint and function names, lower-cased with dashes: api/<module>/<endpoint>/<function>. Open /swagger to see the exact routes, and check that you used the right HTTP verb.That function has no NodeWalker graph yet. Open it in the API Editor, press Open in NodeWalker, build the logic, save, and build the project again.Anything that deletes data is written but commented out, because a rename looks the same as a drop plus an add. Read it, uncomment the lines you mean, and run it.Make sure its folder is in DatabaseDesignerData\<your username>\Row Templates\ or Project Templates\, not inside a project. Templates from versions before 3.0 may need exporting again.Open Themes and press Set Default on Default. If one window is hard to read, use the transparency slider at its top right.

item.title: Welcome
item.description:
A Free, Open Source Solution That Allows You To Create Backends Without Code Database Designer is an offline, no-code PostgreSQL modeling tool that auto-generates SQL, documentation, and C# Entity Framework with PQC-resistant security. Windows • Linux (Soon) • Fully Offline • Post Quantum Computing Resistant • No BS ## How It WorksDatabase Designer provides a visual, schema-first workflow for building application backends. It generates:✅ Complete SQL files — schemas, tables, references, and indexes ready to deploy 📘 Markdown documentation — clean, exportable, and team-friendly 💻 Entity Framework–ready C# classes — plug-and-play with your applicationsInstead of writing raw SQL or juggling migrations manually, you: Design tables visually Define relationships and constraints explicitly Generate schemas, documentation, and code artifacts Keep everything offline and under your control The tool is designed to stay out of your runtime — it helps you design systems, not lock you into them.It also builds a working ASP.NET Core API from the logic you draw in NODEWLKR, with row level security, migrations and a local test database to try it all before you ship.
New here? Start with 1. General Setup. Updating? See What's New In 3.0.
View the source code: Database Designer on GitHub
Hey, you idiot! Don't just stand there staring—get over here already!I'm Masuki-chan, the mascot for this Database Designer thing you've got open. I've been waiting forever for someone to finally use it properly!Designing databases doesn't have to be all boring and tedious like building stupid walls, y'know? With me around, you'll whip up perfect schemas, SQL files, docs, and even C# models in no time! Then you can stop wasting hours and actually focus on creating awesome stuff!You do not link it into your application. You design, export, and implement however you want.Typical workflow: Create or open a project Define schemas and tables Add columns, indexes, and relationships Validate structure Export SQL / docs / models / API Test it on Local Database, then ship No runtime dependency No forced framework No surprises Code:

item.title: 9. Guide - Building A Simple Store
item.description: This guide builds a small but real online store with Database Designer: products with stock, orders, and card payments through Stripe. When you're done you'll have an exported ASP.NET Core API that: lists and searches products, reserves stock safely at checkout (two people can never buy the last item), creates a Stripe payment for the order, marks the order paid only after Stripe confirms it, and lets a buyer cancel an unpaid order and puts the stock back. No hand-written backend code is needed; the logic is built in NodeWalker. You'll need: Database Designer, PostgreSQL, the .NET 8 SDK (to run the exported API), and a free Stripe account (test mode is enough). Shortcut: the finished store ships as a project template. In Projects > Create New Project, press Edit Template and pick Simple Store to get the three tables and all five endpoints with their graphs. Read on to see how each part works, or jump to step 9. Create a new project called Simple Store, then add three tables in the Table Editor, all in the schema store. Use lower-case snake_case names (is_listed, not IsListed). Postgres lower-cases unquoted names, and the build check will warn you if a name would break the API. 10,2 means up to 10 digits with 2 after the decimal point, so prices keep their cents. The stock >= 0 check means the database itself refuses to go below zero.Restrict on product_id stops anyone deleting a product that has orders.Open ER Diagram to check it: you should see three cards with arrows from products.seller_id and orders.buyer_id to users.id, and from orders.product_id to products.id. Already have a database? Import SQL accepts a pg_dump --schema-only file and creates these tables for you. If buyers will connect with their own database role, add RLS in the RLS Editor: Role Standard Users store.products: policy Products, Access Public read, own writes, Owner column seller_id store.orders: policy My orders, Access Own rows, Owner column buyer_id Role Admin Users: store.orders, Access Everyone Each policy row shows an Effective line such as standard_users may ALL only rows where buyer_id = the current user. Check it reads the way you mean.The API in this guide talks to the database as one trusted service account, so RLS is extra protection rather than a requirement. To have requests run under RLS, start each graph with DB: RLS Set User (the buyer's id) and DB: RLS Set Role (standard_users).In the API Editor create module Store with two endpoints:Click Open in NodeWalker on each function to build its logic. A Custom Input block becomes an API parameter. Its value CUSTOMINPUT(long orderId) means "a long called orderId". Simple types (string, long and so on) come from the query string; a table type such as CUSTOMINPUT(orders order) is read from the JSON body on POST. Leave the Db input of database blocks unconnected. The API passes in its own database connection. You don't need DB: Open in an API graph. Tables are referred to by name: a Type Literal of products means the store.products table. A Fail If block ends the request with 400 Bad Request and { "error": "<your message>" }. Show listed products, cheapest first. DB: Query EntityType <- Type Literal products Predicate <- Where: Is True (Property <- String Literal IsListed) OrderBy <- Select: Field (Property <- String Literal Price) Take <- Int Literal 50 Set Output <- DB: Query Rows Property names use the C# spelling, PascalCase: is_listed becomes IsListed. Custom Input = CUSTOMINPUT(string q) Format: Template <- String Literal %{0}%, Arg0 <- Custom Input Where: Like: Property <- Name, Pattern <- Format Result (case-insensitive, % = anything) Where: Is True: Property <- IsListed Where: And: A <- Like, B <- Is True DB: Get Where: EntityType <- Type Literal products, Predicate <- Where: And Set Output <- Rows This graph does the important work: Take the stock in one database statement, so it can't oversell. Price and save the order. Ask Stripe to start a payment. Store the payment id on the order and commit. Custom Input = CUSTOMINPUT(orders order). The client sends {"buyerId": 2, "productId": 1, "quantity": 2}. DB: Begin Tx: everything below is committed together at the end. Two Expose blocks on the Custom Input: ProductId and Quantity. DB: Decrement Where EntityType <- Type Literal products Property <- String Literal Stock Amount <- Expose Quantity Predicate <- Where: And of Where: And ( Where: Equals Id = Expose ProductId, Where: Greater Or Equal Stock ≥ Expose Quantity ), and Where: Is True IsListed This becomes a single SQL statement: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - @qty WHERE id = @id AND stock >= @qty AND is_listed. Two buyers racing for the last item can't both succeed; the second one updates 0 rows. Equals: A <- Decrement Affected, B <- Int Literal 0 Fail If: Condition <- Equals, Message <- String Literal Out of stock DB: Get One By Id: EntityType <- products, Id <- Expose ProductId Expose Price on its Row Multiply: A <- Price, B <- Quantity. This is the order total. Run After: After <- Fail If Ok, Value <- Custom Input. This makes sure nothing is saved unless the stock check passed. Set Field: Object <- Run After Then, Property <- Total, Value <- Multiply Run After: After <- Multiply, Value <- the first Run After's Then DB: Add And Save: Entity <- that Run After Expose Id on Add And Save's Saved output. That's the new order's id. status is already pending (its default) and created_at is filled in by the database. HTTP: New Client Env Var STRIPE_SECRET_KEY -> HTTP: Set Bearer Token (Client, Token) Env Var STRIPE_API_BASE; set it to https://api.stripe.com on the server Format (URL): Template {0}/v1/payment_intents, Arg0 <- Env Var STRIPE_API_BASE Multiply (cents): A <- order total, B <- Int Literal 100 Format (form body): Template amount={0:0}&currency=usd&metadata[order_id]={1}&automatic_payment_methods[enabled]=true with Arg0 <- cents, Arg1 <- Expose Id HTTP: Post Form: Client, Url <- URL Format, Form <- body Format. Stripe expects a form-encoded body, not JSON. HTTP: Read JSON Field ×3 on the response: error.message, id, client_secret Not Equals: A <- error.message, B <- String Literal (empty) -> Fail If (Message <- error.message). This passes Stripe's own error back to the caller. Never put the secret key in the graph. Env Var reads it from the server, so it isn't stored in your project or templates. Run After: After <- the Stripe Fail If Ok, Value <- Read JSON Field id DB: Update Where: EntityType <- orders, Predicate <- Where: Equals Id = order id, Property <- PaymentRef, Value <- that Run After Run After: After <- Update Where Affected, Value <- DB: Begin Tx Tx DB: Commit Tx: Tx <- that Run After Object: Build: orderId <- order id, total <- total, clientSecret <- Read JSON Field client_secret Run After: After <- the commit's Run After, Value <- Object: Build Set Output <- that Run After The response looks like {"orderId": 1, "total": 25, "clientSecret": "pi_..._secret_..."}.The browser tells your API "I paid", but your API checks with Stripe itself. Never trust the browser on this. Custom Input = CUSTOMINPUT(long orderId) DB: Get One By Id (orders, Id <- Custom Input) Equals (Row, Null) -> Fail If Order not found Run After (After <- Fail If Ok, Value <- Row) -> Expose PaymentRef Format {0}/v1/payment_intents/{1} (Arg0 <- Env Var STRIPE_API_BASE, Arg1 <- PaymentRef) HTTP: New Client + Set Bearer Token (Env Var STRIPE_SECRET_KEY) -> HTTP: Get (Url <- Format) HTTP: Read JSON Field status -> Not Equals succeeded -> Fail If Payment not completed yet Run After (After <- that Fail If Ok, Value <- String Literal paid) DB: Update Where: orders, Where: Equals Id = orderId, Property Status, Value <- Run After Object: Build orderId, status, updated -> Set Output Only a pending order can be cancelled, and cancelling puts its stock back exactly once. Custom Input = CUSTOMINPUT(long orderId) DB: Update Where: orders, Predicate <- Where: And (Equals Id = orderId, Equals Status = pending), Property Status, Value cancelled Equals (Affected, 0) -> Fail If Only pending orders can be cancelled Run After (After <- Fail If Ok, Value <- orderId) -> DB: Get One By Id (orders) DB: Increment Where: products, Where: Equals Id = Expose ProductId, Property Stock, Amount <- Expose Quantity Object: Build orderId, restocked -> Set Output Because step 2 only matches a pending order, a second cancel (or cancelling a paid order) updates nothing and stops at the Fail If. Stock can't be restocked twice.Open Build Project and press Build Check. You should see good to go, or only tips. Fix anything listed as an error. Then Export. The export folder GeneratedDB/vN contains:Later, when you change the design, export again and run the new Migration.sql on your existing database instead of rebuilding it. Anything that would delete data is left commented out for you to review.Open Local Database on the desktop: Enter your Postgres connection (for example Host=localhost;Port=5432;Username=postgres;Password=yourpassword;Database=shop) and press Test & save. The database is created if it doesn't exist. Create from scratch runs SQL.sql and RLS.sql from your latest export. Add sample data fills every table with believable rows (parents before children, so foreign keys line up). Or run your own INSERTs in the query box. Set STRIPE_SECRET_KEY (and STRIPE_API_BASE=https://api.stripe.com) as environment variables, then Start API. Swagger opens when it's ready. You can also test one endpoint without the API: open its graph in NodeWalker and press ▶ Run. Fill in the inputs (for Checkout: {"buyerId":2,"productId":1,"quantity":2}) and you'll see the result, or the error and which block caused it. Database changes are rolled back unless you tick Keep database changes, even though Checkout commits its own transaction.createdb shop psql shop -f SQL.sql psql shop -f RLS.sql # if you added RLS Seed a seller and a product:INSERT INTO store.users (username, email) VALUES ('alice', 'alice@example.com'), ('bob', 'bob@example.com'); INSERT INTO store.products (seller_id, name, price, stock) VALUES (1, 'Desk Lamp', 12.50, 3); Then, from the API folder:export ConnectionStrings__Default="Host=localhost;Database=shop;Username=postgres;Password=yourpassword" export STRIPE_SECRET_KEY=sk_test_yourkey # Stripe Dashboard > Developers > API keys (test mode) export STRIPE_API_BASE=https://api.stripe.com dotnet run Swagger opens at /swagger. Try it:curl http://localhost:5000/api/store/products/list curl -X POST http://localhost:5000/api/store/orders/checkout \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"buyerId":2,"productId":1,"quantity":2}' Checkout returned a clientSecret. With Stripe.js:<script src="https://js.stripe.com/v3/"></script> <div id="payment"></div><button id="pay">Pay</button> <script type="module"> const stripe = Stripe('pk_test_yourkey'); // publishable key const { orderId, clientSecret } = await (await fetch('/api/store/orders/checkout', { method: 'POST', headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify({ buyerId: 2, productId: 1, quantity: 1 }) })).json(); const elements = stripe.elements({ clientSecret }); elements.create('payment').mount('#payment'); document.getElementById('pay').onclick = async () => { const { error } = await stripe.confirmPayment({ elements, redirect: 'if_required' }); if (!error) await fetch(`/api/store/orders/confirm?orderId=${orderId}`, { method: 'POST' }); }; </script> In test mode use card 4242 4242 4242 4242, any future date, any CVC. Webhooks: also call your Confirm logic from a Stripe payment_intent.succeeded webhook, so an order is marked paid even if the buyer closes the tab. Expiring holds: cancel pending orders older than, say, 30 minutes. A DB: Query with Where: Less on CreatedAt plus the Cancel steps does it. Sellers: a GET orders/for-seller endpoint with Where: Equals on the product's SellerId. Several items per order: an order_items table referencing orders; checkout repeats step 6a per item inside the same transaction.
item.guid: Tutorials For Building/9. Guide - Building A Simple Store.md

item.title: 10. Personalizing With Themes
item.description:
Themes recolor the login screen, the desktop, projects, tables, the designer and more. Every window reads from the same small palette, so switching a theme repaints all of it at once. A theme can also set a background wallpaper.Database Designer starts on the Default theme, which looks the way the app always has. It also comes with a few other themes you can switch to whenever you like, including a Y2K Chrome look with a frutiger-aqua wallpaper.
💜 Default is the default. Themes are opt-in! Out of the box you get the plain Default look. Nothing changes until you pick a theme. Fancy something different? Apply one of the built-ins, or make your own in about a minute. And you can always flip back to Default. Keep reading, dummy. 🐰 From the main desktop, open the Themes app.
The Themes window lists every theme you have. Each theme has two buttons: Apply switches to that theme right now, just for this session. Set Default applies it and remembers it, so it loads every time you start Database Designer. The theme currently set as your default is marked with a DEFAULT pill.
A theme is just a folder with a theme.json file inside it. Open DatabaseDesignerData\<your username>\Themes\. The built-in themes live here too. Make a new folder named whatever you want your theme to be called, e.g. My Theme. Inside it, create a theme.json like this: { "Colors": { "Theme_BackgroundColor": "#1D1A6B", "Theme_TextOnPrimaryColor": "#E6F4FF", "Theme_TextBrush": "#161257" }, "BackgroundImage": "background.jpg" } What the keys mean: Colors are hex, #RRGGBB, or #AARRGGBB if you want transparency. BackgroundImage is optional. Put an image (.jpg or .png) next to theme.json and name it here, or leave it out for a color-only theme. Wallpapers fill the screen without stretching. On very wide or very tall screens the edges are cropped instead. Back in the Themes app, your theme now shows up in the list. Press Apply to try it, or Set Default to keep it.
💜 Tip: start from a copy! The easiest way to make your own is to copy the Y2K Chrome folder, rename the copy, and tweak the three colors until it looks right. You can't break anything: a bad color just falls back to a safe default. Go wild! 🌟
Y2K icons on this page are from Twemoji (© Twitter, CC-BY 4.0).
item.guid: Tutorials For Users/10. Personalizing With Themes.md

item.title: 7. Exporting Your Project And Creating Templates
item.description:
The Build Project page checks your project, builds everything you need to run it (SQL, security rules, C# and an API), and makes templates you can reuse or share. Open Build Project from the desktop. Press Build Check.
Build Check lists errors (would break the SQL or the API), warnings (probably mistakes) and tips. Click any line to open the table it's about. Fix the errors, then press Build Check again until they're gone. The full list of what it checks is in 1. Building Your Projects. Press Export. Press Build Project. Each build goes into a new numbered folder (GeneratedDB\v1, v2 and so on) inside your project folder, so nothing is overwritten:
Press View Builds to open the folder. To try the build on your own computer, see 7. Testing With Local Database.
A table template packs some of your tables (with their columns, references and indexes) so you can add them to other projects. Press Export Specific Rows. Templates tab: pick the tables. Each one shows up on the right, where you can give it a description. Pack Information tab: a banner (optional), the template name and an overview. Author tab: your name, plus an optional picture, company, website, license and note. Finalize tab: check the preview and press Finalize. The list on the Finalize tab tells you what's still missing and updates as you type. The name can't contain \ / : * ? " < > | because it becomes a folder name.Templates are saved to DatabaseDesignerData\<your username>\Row Templates\<Template Name>\v1\. Building the same name again makes v2, v3 and so on, and the newest one is used.
To use one, press Use A Template when creating a table. The full guide is in 5. Templates.
A project template is a copy of a whole project that new projects can start from. Press Export Template. Pick the project. Fill in the same information as for table templates. Press Finalize. It's saved to DatabaseDesignerData\<your username>\Project Templates\<Template Name>\ with the project's tables, RLS, API design, NodeWalker graphs, icon and wallpaper.
💜 Exports are readable! Templates and exported projects aren't scrambled with your account key, so you can open them, see exactly what's inside, and send them to a friend who can actually use them. When you import something it gets encrypted for your account, so your working copy stays private. Your projects are saved encrypted with your account, so you can't just copy the folder to someone else. To share one: Open Projects and press Export (Portable) on the project's card. This writes DatabaseDesignerData\<your username>\Exports\<Project Name>.ddproject (and a folder with the same contents). Send the .ddproject file. Your Local Database connection is never included. Put the .ddproject file (or an exported project folder) in DatabaseDesignerData\<your username>\Imports\. Open Projects and press Import Project. Each one becomes a new project, encrypted for your account. Imported files are moved to Imports\Imported\, so pressing Import twice doesn't make copies. If you already have a project with that name, a number is added (My Project (2)), so nothing gets overwritten.
💜 Free backups! A .ddproject file is a full backup of your project. Keep one somewhere safe, and if anything goes wrong, drop it back into Imports\ and press Import Project. Easy! Every account starts with these, so you have working examples to learn from:Table templates (press Use A Template when creating a table):Project templates (press Edit Template when creating a project):They're normal templates: open them, change them, or use them as a reference for your own. Run Build Check first. It catches broken references before they break your SQL. Give templates clear names and overviews. They're what people see when picking one. A banner and author picture make your template easy to spot in the list. Templates are versioned for you (v1, v2...), so you can keep improving one without losing the old version.
item.guid: Tutorials For Users/7. Exporting Your Project And Creating Templates.md

item.title: 6. Adding Data To Your First Table
item.description:
In the Table Editor, click a table to open it in the Database Viewer. Its columns are listed in the middle, and clicking one shows its details on the right, where you can edit or delete it.At the top are three buttons: add a column, add an index and add a reference. Each one opens a step-by-step form.A column holds one piece of data for every row, like a name, a price or a date. The form asks: The basics: the column's name and description. The data type: Text, Integer, BigInt, Boolean, Numeric, TimestampTz, JsonB and so on. Some types take a length: 50 on a VarChar means at most 50 characters, and 10,2 on a Numeric means up to 10 digits with 2 after the decimal point. What it is: whether it's the primary key, unique, required (Not Null), an array, or media / encrypted data. Default value and check constraints: a value to use when none is given (like 0 or 'pending'), and a rule every row must follow (like price >= 0). If the default is a Postgres function such as now(), answer Yes when it asks.
Every table needs a primary key, usually a column called id of type BigSerial (a number that counts up by itself).An index makes searching on a column faster. Add one to columns you often filter or sort by, like email or created_at.
A reference (foreign key) links a column to a row in another table, like an order pointing at the user who placed it.Pick the target in two columns: tables on the left, that table's columns on the right. Only columns a reference can point at are shown: the primary key, or a column marked Unique. If a column's type doesn't match yours, it's flagged with the type you need. Both sides must be the same type, for example both BigInt. When you edit an existing reference, it shows what it points at now. Then choose what happens when the row it points at is deleted or updated:
Press Ctrl+Z to undo and Ctrl+Y to redo. This works for columns, indexes, references and whole tables.To delete your table, click the Delete Table button twice within 10 seconds.
item.guid: Tutorials For Users/6. Adding Data To Your First Table.md

item.title: 5. Creating Your First Table And Using The Table Viewer
item.description:
To begin, start by clicking "Table Editor". You will see a UI similar to the file editor appear.💜Hard To Read? Change The Transparency!
Sometimes, it might be hard to see what's happening because of what's going on in the background! To change this, slide the slider at the top right to change the transparency of the background! You can change transparency for windows separately, allowing you to prioritize some and ignore others if need be! Click the + button to open the table creation UI. You have the option of creating a completely new table and schema, or using a template.There must not be a table with the same name at the same schema. Enter Schema (optional) – Leave blank for "public" schema. Use quotes for multi-part schemas (e.g., "my.schema"). Enter Table Name – Dots and spaces are automatically converted to underscores. Add Description (optional) – Describe the table's purpose. Click Finalize to create an empty table. You can add columns, indexes, and relationships afterward. Press Use A Template to open the template browser. Find the pack you want and press Select Template Pack.
The pack's tables (with their columns, indexes and references) are added to your project with their own names. If a table with the same schema and name already exists, it's skipped and you're told which ones were. More on templates in 5. Templates. Names may contain: letters, numbers, underscores, parentheses, hyphens, equals, plus, commas, colons, semicolons, slashes, backslashes, exclamation, question marks, @, square brackets, curly braces, spaces, periods, and double quotes. Duplicate schema‑qualified table names are not allowed. Even though more is allowed, stick to lower-case letters, numbers and underscores (like order_items). Postgres lower-cases names you don't quote, and Build Check warns about names that would cause trouble in SQL or the API. From here, you can go back to the Table Editor. There are a few options you have;You can type at the top to find certain items, clicking the reload button to update the UI and clicking search will look for items.Typing Schema.Na will for example show"Schema_Name.Table" "Schema_Name.Table2" "Schema_Name_Goes.Table" and "Schema_Nap.Table"You can go back and forth between your searches through the button to the left of the inputfield to search through items.The Home and Downloads entries on the left don't do anything yet.

Import SQL turns an existing Postgres schema into tables. See 13. Notes, ER Diagram And Import SQL. ER Diagram shows all your tables and how they connect. Click a table's title there to open it.
item.guid: Tutorials For Users/5. Creating Your First Table And Using The Table Viewer.md

item.title: 4. Customizing Your Project
item.description:
You can get a general overview of your project anytime by clicking the "General Projects" button on the desktop.Clicking Clear Screen removes all UI objects from it besides the basics; very useful for when you have a lot of pages open on your screen!Clicking Set Wallpaper opens the file browser, allowing you to replace the BG with your own.
This supports PNGs, JPGs and GIFs. The project will also remember the wallpaper you select the next time you open it. Wallpapers fill the screen without being stretched, so they look right on ultra-wide monitors too (the edges are cropped instead).Atop this, you can click "Edit Project". This will allow you to set the name of the project, the biography for it and a logo for it. The logo will auto update as soon as it's changed and can be a .PNG, .JPG or .GIF.
You can also delete the project, which will send you back to a "No Project Selected" scene.The next time you open the projects list or information window, you will see the updates.

item.title: 2. Logging In And Music
item.description:
Go to the startup screen once more and click login, then find your account
Enter your password into the field and click enter

💜 Error 500??? Completely Normal Database Designer's security exists on a completely local API due to the goals around programming it earlier on! When a login error occurs, it appears as an Error 500 for this reason! Not to fear, it realistically means (Most Common) You typed in the wrong password There is an error with accessing the directory Database Designer is installed into or The backend API isn't working (Unlikely since the login screen wouldn't pop up when you click it) Once logged in, you can close the login screen!
On the login screen, press Forgot Password? / Change Password. You can set a new password with either: your recovery code (the one you saved when you made the account), or your current password, if you just want to change it. Your projects are re-encrypted with the new password, and a backup of the old copies is kept in DatabaseDesignerData\<your username>\Backups\ just in case.Accounts made before recovery codes existed get one the first time they log in. It's only shown once, so save it!Wanting to change the volume of the music playing? Beyond Alt + M, you can look to the bottom right bar to see the settings available to you!Clicking the first will set the volume to 0 whereas the second will open or close the volume slider.
Click the music note on the lower bar to open the Music Player. It has two tabs: Become As Dust Album: the BECOME AS D[U]ST album, 20 songs composed by WalkerDev, based off of Nier, Muv-Luv and other media. My Music: the songs in your computer's Music folder. Click a folder to open it and Up to go back. .mp3, .wav, .flac, .aac and .m4a files all play.
A few things worth knowing: Music keeps playing when you close the player. Open it again and it shows what's playing. Every song shows how many times you've played it. A play counts when the song finishes, and every time it repeats with Loop on. Loop repeats the current song and Shuffle picks the next one at random. The volume slider and seeking work for your own songs too. Play counts are saved per account.
item.guid: Tutorials For Users/2. Logging In And Music.md

item.title: 1. General Setup
item.description:
You can find Database Designer on Steam or
Itch.io Start by launching Database Designer For Steam, you can simply head to your library and click "Start". For Itch.io, go to the location you extracted the .zip file to and click "Database Designer.exe" Leave the opening CMD to startup; this is completely part of Database Designer and handles a few things at the backend
At this point, you will be at the starting screen!
💜 Hotkeys Exist In Database Designer! Database Designer has two shortcuts you can use from the start! Alt + M will (m)ute the sounds
Alt + L will toggle the (l)ower bar's visibility Database Designer uses a background server to run the security logic and it seems that firewalls don't like this! You might see that the login button is not clickable. You just have to whitelist Database Designer and Pariah API.exe on your firewalls! Pariah API.exe is the security API that actually handles encrypting and saving information. You will find it in the Database Designer folder under Assets/Pariah API/Pariah API.exe, and you can look at the code here for any concerns you might have! https://github.com/Walker-Industries-RnD/PariahCybersecurity ### 3. Creating an account To create an account with Database Designer, start by clicking the login button and create user.

Now, set a username and password. The password must have an uppercase and lowercase letter, a symbol and be 12+ characters long. It's important to click "Continue" when done and not just switch to another tab.

💜 Switching Tabs Resets Login Data! It may not look like it, but every time you switch back to the Basics Tab, the Username and Password information is reset! You will have to reenter the information and click continue. "But Why?" Mainly to help make sure your credentials are secured! Select an avatar PFP and click continue.
Validate the information entered; if it looks good, click Finalize.

Take the recovery code from the next page and save it somewhere secure. If you ever forget your password, this code is the only way to set a new one (see 2. Logging In And Music). Press Copy To Clipboard first so you don't have to type it out. Do not share this code with ANYONE.
Undo and redo cover tables, references, indexes, RLS, the API design and notes, up to 100 steps per project. Moving windows around doesn't count as a change. When you undo, windows that show project data close so nothing keeps editing the old copy.
NodeWalker has its own shortcuts, listed in 2. NODEWLKR.

item.title: 8. Migrations
item.description: Once your database has real data in it, you can't just drop it and run SQL.sql again. Migration.sql upgrades the database you already have to match your latest design.Every build saves a schema.snapshot.json next to its SQL. The next build compares your project with that snapshot and writes Migration.sql: the statements that turn a database built from the previous build into one that matches this build.So GeneratedDB\v5\Migration.sql upgrades a database built from v4. new tables and new columns changed types, defaults, Not Null, Unique and Check constraints new and removed foreign keys new and removed indexes Everything runs in one transaction. If any statement fails, nothing is changed.Dropping a table or a column deletes data, and a rename looks exactly like a drop plus an add. So those statements are written but commented out. Read them, uncomment the ones you really mean, and for a rename, replace the drop and add with:ALTER TABLE store.products RENAME COLUMN title TO name; Changing which column is the primary key is also left to you. The migration lists it at the top with the statements you'll need. In Database Designer: Local Database > Apply Migration.sql. By hand: psql -d yourdatabase -f Migration.sql. Run RLS.sql again afterwards if you changed any policies. It's safe to run more than once. Build after each set of changes, so each migration stays small and easy to read. Skipped a version? Run each migration in order (v4, then v5, then v6). Adding a Not Null column to a table that already has rows needs a default, or the migration will fail on the existing rows. Always try a migration on Local Database before running it on a live database.

item.title: 5. Templates
item.description: Templates let you reuse tables and whole projects instead of building them again. There are two kinds: Table templates (also called row templates): one or more tables, with their columns, references and indexes. Project templates: a whole project, including RLS, the API design and every NodeWalker graph. Templates belong to your account, not to one project, so a template you make is offered in every project. Open Table Editor and press +. Press Use A Template. Find the pack you want and press Select Template Pack. The pack's tables are added to the open project. A table that already exists in the project (same schema and name) is left alone, and you're told which ones were skipped. Afterwards you can edit the new tables like any other. Open Projects and press Create New Project. Press Edit Template and pick a project template. You can also pick table templates here to add on top. Give the project a name and description and press Enter. Open Build Project and press Export Specific Rows. The form has four tabs: Templates: pick the tables to include. Each one you pick shows up on the right, where you can give it a description. Pack Information: a banner (optional, 1500x200), the template name and an overview. Author: your name, plus an optional picture, company, website, license and note. Finalize: check the preview and press Finalize. The list on the Finalize tab says what's still missing and updates as you type. A name can't contain any of \ / : * ? " < > |, because it becomes a folder name.The template is saved to:DatabaseDesignerData\<your username>\Row Templates\<Template Name>\v1\ Building a template with the same name again makes v2, v3 and so on. The newest version is the one offered when you use it. Open Build Project and press Export Template. Pick the project. Fill in the same information as above and press Finalize. It's saved to DatabaseDesignerData\<your username>\Project Templates\<Template Name>\, together with the project's session.json, its Scripts folder (your NodeWalker graphs), its icon and its wallpaper.These are installed the first time you log in. Installing never overwrites a template you've changed.Simple Store is the finished version of 9. Guide - Building A Simple Store.Templates are saved unencrypted, so you can open them, check what's inside and send them to someone else. To install one, copy its folder into your own Row Templates or Project Templates folder.Templates made with versions before 3.0 may not load. If one gives you trouble, delete its folder and export it again.

item.title: 4. No Code RLS
item.description: RLS lets the database itself decide which rows each user can see and change, so a bug in your API can't leak someone else's data. For a walkthrough of the editor, see 11. Securing Your Data With The RLS Editor. This page covers what gets generated and how to use it.Each policy in the RLS Editor has:When the owner column is empty, the first of these that exists on the table is used: user_id, owner_id, created_by, author_id, seller_id, account_id, profile_id, member_id, sender_id, buyer_id, customer_id. On a table whose name contains "user", "account" or "profile", the primary key is used. If nothing fits, the editor warns you, because then only admins would see the rows.Under each policy is a line that says in plain words what it allows, for example "standard_users may SELECT only rows where user_id = the current user (admins/moderators bypass)". A database role for each role in the editor. Standard Users becomes standard_users. Helper functions: current_user_id(), is_admin() and is_moderator(). ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on every table that has policies. The policies themselves, plus the GRANTs each role needs. Admins can read and write every row. Moderators can read every row but only write their own. Everyone else gets what their policies allow.RLS.sql drops and recreates its policies, so it's safe to run again after every build. Run it after SQL.sql.The policies read two settings: the current user's id and their role. Set both at the start of every request, on the same connection:SELECT set_config('app.current_user_id', '42', false); SELECT set_config('role', 'standard_users', false); In NodeWalker, the DB: RLS Set User and DB: RLS Set Role blocks do exactly this. DB: RLS Reset User clears them again.Superusers, and roles with BYPASSRLS, ignore every policy. If you connect your API as postgres, RLS does nothing. Make a normal login role that is a member of the generated roles and connect with that.Pick Custom SQL when the other options don't fit. You write the USING part (which rows can be seen or changed) and optionally the WITH CHECK part (which rows can be written). For example:user_id = current_user_id() OR is_public Every policy also has an Open in NodeWalker button. RLS.sql is built from the settings above, not from the graph, so use the graph for extra logic you want to keep next to the policy.
item.guid: Tutorials For Building/4. No Code RLS.md

item.title: 3. No Code API
item.description:
The API Editor is where you plan your API, and NodeWalker is where you build what each part does. When you build the project, both turn into a real ASP.NET Core API. For a walkthrough of the editor itself, see 12. Designing Your API With The API Editor.Names are lower-cased and spaces become dashes, so a module called User Accounts becomes api/user-accounts.Each function with a NodeWalker graph becomes a controller action that runs that graph. The graph's inputs become request parameters: Simple values (numbers, text, true/false, ids) come from the query string. On POST, PUT and PATCH, one object input (for example a whole order) comes from the JSON body. Name your inputs with CUSTOMINPUT(long orderId) so the parameter is called orderId instead of something generic. If a graph uses Fail If, the API answers 400 Bad Request with your message. Functions without a graph get a placeholder that answers "Not implemented yet", so the API still builds while you work on it.GeneratedDB/vN/API/ ├── API.csproj # Project file (.NET 8) ├── Program.cs # Startup, database connection and Swagger ├── appsettings.json # Connection string ├── Controllers/ │ ├── {Module}Controller.cs │ └── Logic/ # C# compiled from your NodeWalker graphs └── Models/ # Entity Framework models and DbContext Models are generated from your tables. Column defaults carry over: a default like 'pending' becomes the C# default, and now() is left for the database to fill in. Optional columns are nullable, and array columns become arrays. Swagger is always on, so every route can be tried from the browser at /swagger. Install the .NET SDK (8 or newer). Put your database connection in appsettings.json under ConnectionStrings:Default, or set the ConnectionStrings__Default environment variable. In the API folder, run dotnet run.
Or skip all of that and press Start API in Local Database, which runs it against your local database and opens Swagger for you. See 7. Testing With Local Database.Never type an API key into a String Literal. Use the Env Var block and set the variable where the API runs. The Simple Store template does this for its Stripe key (STRIPE_SECRET_KEY).
item.guid: Tutorials For Building/3. No Code API.md

item.title: 1. Building Your Projects
item.description:
Building turns your project into files you can actually use: the SQL for your database, the security rules, C# classes, documentation and a working API. Open Build Project from the desktop. Press Build Check and fix anything it reports. Press Export, then Build Project. Press View Builds to open the folder with the results. Build Check goes through the whole project and sorts what it finds into three kinds: Errors would break the SQL or the API. Fix these before you export. Warnings are probably mistakes. Tips are worth a look but won't break anything. Click a line to open that table. It catches: duplicate tables or columns, and tables without a primary key reserved words used as names (order, user and so on) and column names with capital letters foreign keys whose types don't match, that point at a column that isn't unique, or that use ON DELETE SET NULL on a Not Null column foreign keys that go round in a circle, and indexes on columns that don't exist RLS policies for tables that don't exist or that have no owner column Every build goes into a new numbered folder, so older builds are never overwritten.{ProjectFolder}/ └── GeneratedDB/ └── v1/ ├── SQL.sql # Tables, keys, references and indexes ├── RLS.sql # Roles, row level security policies and helper functions ├── Migration.sql # Upgrades a database built from the previous build ├── schema.snapshot.json # Used to work out the next Migration.sql ├── Documentation.md # Every table and column, with your descriptions ├── Classes.cs # C# classes for your tables ├── Models.cs # Entity Framework DbContext ├── API/ # ASP.NET Core API with Swagger │ ├── API.csproj │ ├── Program.cs │ ├── appsettings.json │ ├── Controllers/ │ └── Models/ └── SpacetimeDB/ # Reserved for a SpacetimeDB module (empty for now) RLS.sql is safe to run more than once. Migration.sql is explained in 8. Migrations.
The API is explained in 3. No Code API.
To try all of it on your own machine, see 7. Testing With Local Database.
Export Template saves the whole project as a project template, and Export Specific Rows saves some of its tables as a table template. Both are covered in 5. Templates.
item.guid: Tutorials For Building/1. Building Your Projects.md

item.title: 2. NODEWLKR
item.description: NodeWalker is the node editor that holds the logic behind your API functions and RLS policies. You place blocks, wire them together, and NodeWalker turns the graph into C#. When you build your project, that C# goes into the exported API, so the graph you draw is the code that runs.You don't open NodeWalker on its own. Every function in the API Editor and every policy in the RLS Editor has an Open in NodeWalker button, and each one gets its own graph.Every block has: a title that says what it does inputs on the left (what it needs) outputs on the right (what it gives back) sometimes a Value you type in, like the text of a String Literal or the field name for a Where block Click a block to open it in the Node Inspector on the right, where you can edit its value and see its inputs and outputs.Drag from an output to an input to connect them. A data wire says where a value comes from: "the Count input of this block is the output of that block". Yellow dot: required input. The block won't compile without it. Red dot: optional input. If you leave it empty, a default (0, empty text, false) is used. Purple dot: a custom type, like one of your table classes. To remove a wire, click it and press Delete, or right-click it and pick Delete Connection.Blocks that do something (save to the database, set a variable, fail the request) have white pins: In on the left and Then on the right. A flow wire says which block runs next.Data wires answer "where does this value come from?" and flow wires answer "what happens next?". You need both once your logic has steps that depend on a condition or happen in a loop.Graphs without any flow wires still work. NodeWalker works out the order from the data wires, the same as older versions did.Graphs that come from a template are laid out automatically the first time you open them, left to right in the order they run. Move things wherever you like afterwards; your layout is saved.The right-click menu on the canvas also has Check Warnings (lists inputs that still need wiring), Manage Usings... (extra using lines for the generated file) and Import Entity....A few rules: A Then pin leads to one block. If you want several things to happen, use Sequence. Several paths can lead into the same block. If both sides of a Branch lead to the same block, it runs after the if/else. Flow pins only connect to flow pins, and data pins only to data pins. Value blocks (math, comparisons, Where blocks, Get Variable) are worked out right where they are used. A Get Variable inside a loop reads the latest value every time round. If a block reads a value that only exists on another path (for example the Item of a For Each, used after the loop), View Code shows a warning above the code. Equals, Not Equals, Less Than, Greater Than, Less Or Equal and Greater Or Equal compare any two values: Numbers are compared by value, so an int and a decimal compare fine (5 equals 5.0). Text that holds a number is treated as that number, so "10" is greater than 9. Dates are compared as dates. Anything else is compared as text. An empty (null) value is smaller than everything else and only equals another null. Before 3.0, some of these threw errors like "Object must be of type Double" when the two sides had different types. That's fixed. Graphs made in older versions pick up the fix the next time you build.These replace the old freeform Lambda block. Instead of typing x => x.Price > 10 you build the condition from blocks: Where: Equals, Not Equals, Greater, Less, Greater Or Equal, Less Or Equal, Contains, Starts With, Ends With, Like, Is Null, Is Not Null, Is True, Is False, Between and In. Each one takes a field name (the column) and, where it makes sense, a value. Where: And, Where: Or and Where: Not combine conditions. Select: Field picks the column to sort or read by. DB: Query filters, sorts and pages in one block. DB: Select Field reads one column from the matching rows, and DB: Delete Where deletes them. Plug a Where block into the Predicate input of DB: Get Where, DB: Get First, DB: Count, DB: Query and the other database blocks.For lists you already have (rows you loaded earlier, or a list from the request body): List: Filter, List: First Where, List: Any Where, List: Count Where, List: Sort By, List: Map Field and List: Sum Field. They take the same Where blocks as the database ones.A Custom Input adds a parameter to the generated function. Set its value to CUSTOMINPUT(long) to give it a type, or CUSTOMINPUT(long orderId) to give it a name as well. Named inputs become named request parameters in the exported API.DB: RLS Set User and DB: RLS Set Role tell the database who is making the request, so the policies from the RLS Editor apply. Use them at the start of any graph that reads or writes rows that belong to a user.▶ Run runs the graph you're editing against your Local Database (see 7. Testing With Local Database). It uses the tables from your latest export. Set up a database in Local Database and build it from your export. In NodeWalker, press ▶ Run. Fill in the inputs. Each box starts with an example of what it expects. Press Run. You get the result as JSON, or the error and the name of the block that failed. Changes to the database are rolled back afterwards unless you tick Keep database changes. That includes graphs that commit their own transaction. Run needs the .NET SDK installed.Graphs are saved inside the project, in its Scripts folder, one file per API function or RLS policy. They're included in portable exports and project templates, so your logic travels with the project."Required input not connected" Wire every yellow input, or give it a literal value.The code has a warning about a value from another path A block is using a value that only exists inside a loop or on one side of a Branch. Move the block onto that path, or store the value with Set Variable and read it back with Get Variable.Cycle detected Some data wires go round in a circle. Use a flow block (Repeat or For Each) for loops instead of wiring a block back into itself.Run says it can't find the database or the SDK Set up the connection in Local Database first, build the database from an export, and check that dotnet --version works in a terminal.

item.title: 9. Understanding 3NF
item.description: 3NF means: "Don't repeat information that doesn't need to be repeated. If something can be looked up from another table, put it there instead."Imagine you're building a database to organize everything in the Muv-Luv universe — cadets, their TSF mechs, squadrons, etc.You stuff everything into one giant table:Problems: "Valkyries" is repeated over and over. "Japanese" shows up every single time someone uses a Japanese TSF. "Lieutenant" is copied for everyone with Takemikazuchi. If the UN decides to rename all Japanese TSFs to "Imperial Guard Type", you have to change it in every single row. One mistake and your data is broken forever. Adding a new Valkyrie cadet? Type "Valkyries" and "Japanese" again. So annoying. This is redundant and dangerous; your data will be CHOMP'd because you forgot to update one row.Split repeating info into its own tables.Now it's perfect: Change the squadron name once → fixed everywhere. Rename all Japanese TSFs? Just edit one row in the TSF table. Add a new cadet to Valkyries piloting Takemikazuchi? Just put Squadron ID 10 and TSF ID 30. No typing the same words again. Everything stays clean, no repeats, and changing one thing doesn't break the whole database.
